item.title: “I do not see any other contact, monks, that so obsesses and occupies the mind of a man as the contact of a woman. The…
item.description:
“I do not see any other contact, monks, that so obsesses and occupies the mind of a man as the contact of a woman. The contact of a woman, monks, obsesses and occupies the mind of a man.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.5

item.title: “Householder, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in…
item.description:
“Householder, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in those forms, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them, not depending on them, consciousness arises without clinging to them. Householder, a monk without clinging attains complete Nibbāna … Householder, there are tastes … Householder, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in those phenomena, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — because he does not delight, does not praise, and dwells without lust, not depending on them, consciousness arises without clinging to them. Without clinging, householder, that monk attains Nibbāna. This, householder, is the cause, this is the reason why some beings here and now attain complete Nibbāna.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.124

item.title: “Householder, having known that sensual desire is a defilement of the mind, that noble disciple abandons sensual desire, the defilement of the mind; having known…
item.description:
“Householder, having known that sensual desire is a defilement of the mind, that noble disciple abandons sensual desire, the defilement of the mind; having known that ill-will is a defilement of the mind, he abandons ill-will; having known that sloth and torpor are defilements of the mind, he abandons sloth and torpor; having known that restlessness and remorse are defilements of the mind, he abandons restlessness and remorse; having known that doubt is a defilement of the mind, he abandons doubt. This, householder, is called a noble disciple of great wisdom, of broad wisdom, who has entered the sphere of clear vision, endowed with wisdom. This is called being endowed with wisdom.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.61

item.title: “Monks, what is a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future? Monks, there are some ascetics…
item.description:
“Monks, what is a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future? Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine, such a view: ‘There is no fault in sensual pleasures.’ They indulge in sensual pleasures. Having indulged, at the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a plane of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell. There they experience painful, sharp, severe feelings. They say: ‘Those venerable ascetics and brahmins who see the future danger in sensual pleasures, who speak of the abandoning of sensual pleasures, who describe the full understanding of sensual pleasures—but we, with these sensual pleasures as the cause, as the condition, experience these painful, sharp, severe feelings.’ Monks, this is called a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 45 – Cūḷadhammasamādānasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are agreeable and disagreeable. Though they touch the mind again and again, they do not overpower…
item.description:
“Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are agreeable and disagreeable. Though they touch the mind again and again, they do not overpower the mind and remain. Because the mind is not overpowered, energy and exertion arise, not laziness; mindfulness is established, not lost; the body becomes tranquil, not feverish; the mind becomes concentrated and one-pointed. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness, monks, regarding these monks, I declare that one should strive heedfully with regard to the six sense bases. Monks, there are sounds … odors … tastes … touches … Monks, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are agreeable and disagreeable. Though they touch the mind again and again, they do not overpower the mind and remain. Because the mind is not overpowered, energy and exertion arise, not laziness; mindfulness is established, not lost; the body becomes tranquil, not feverish; the mind becomes concentrated and one-pointed. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness, monks, regarding these monks, I declare that one should strive heedfully with regard to the six sense bases.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.134

item.title: “Good, Māgandiya. I too have never seen or heard of such a one. But, Māgandiya, those ascetics or brahmins who have dwelt, dwell, or will…
item.description:
“Good, Māgandiya. I too have never seen or heard of such a one. But, Māgandiya, those ascetics or brahmins who have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell with craving cut off and mind inwardly peaceful—all of them, having known as they actually are the origination, the passing away, the gratification, the peril, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, with craving for sensual pleasures abandoned and the fever of sensual pleasures removed, have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell with craving cut off and mind inwardly peaceful.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 75 – Māgandiyasutta

item.title: “Monks, abandon one thing. I guarantee you no further rebirth. What one thing? Greed, monks, is that one thing. Abandon it! I guarantee you no…
item.description:
“Monks, abandon one thing. I guarantee you no further rebirth. What one thing? Greed, monks, is that one thing. Abandon it! I guarantee you no further rebirth.” The Blessed One spoke this meaning. Here it is said:

With greed, beings,
Infatuated, go to a bad destination.
But the meditator, with right knowledge,
Abandons that greed.
Having abandoned it, he never
Returns to this world again.

From: Itivuttaka 1

item.title: “Great king, there are three things in the world which, when they arise, lead to harm, suffering, and discomfort. What three? Great king, greed is…
item.description:
“Great king, there are three things in the world which, when they arise, lead to harm, suffering, and discomfort. What three? Great king, greed is a thing in the world which, when it arises, leads to harm, suffering, and discomfort. Great king, hatred is a thing in the world which, when it arises, leads to harm, suffering, and discomfort. Great king, delusion is a thing in the world which, when it arises, leads to harm, suffering, and discomfort. These three things in the world, when they arise, bring harm, suffering, and discomfort.

Greed, hatred, delusion — these three,
Are evil minds for a person,
They damage one’s own self,
They produce one’s own self,
Like the rind and core of a tree,
Producing its own fruit.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.23

item.title: Then Māra, having transformed himself into a brahmin with a large topknot, wearing an antelope skin, old, bent like a rafter, breathing heavily, carrying a…
item.description:
Then Māra, having transformed himself into a brahmin with a large topknot, wearing an antelope skin, old, bent like a rafter, breathing heavily, carrying a udumbara staff, approached those monks. Having approached, he said to them:
- “Venerable sirs, you have gone forth too young, in the prime of youth, with black hair, in the bloom of youth, at the early stage of life, without having enjoyed sensual pleasures. Venerable sirs, enjoy human sensual pleasures. Do not abandon the present to chase after what is subject to time.”

- “Brahmin, we do not abandon the present to chase after what is subject to time. And, brahmin, we abandon what is subject to time to chase after the present. The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are subject to time, of great suffering, of great despair — the peril in them is even greater. This Dhamma is visible here and now, not subject to time, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be directly experienced by the wise.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.21
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Through lust for form, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With form as its object, with form as its support, seeking delight, it grows,…
item.description:
“Through lust for form, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With form as its object, with form as its support, seeking delight, it grows, increases, and expands. Through lust for feeling … for perception … for formations, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With formations as its object, with formations as its support, seeking delight, it grows, increases, and expands. Monks, if anyone says: ‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from formations, I will show the coming and going, the passing away and arising, the growth, increase, and expansion of consciousness’ — such a thing is not possible. Monks, if a monk has abandoned lust for the form element — with the abandonment of lust, the basis is cut off, the support of consciousness does not exist. Monks, if he has abandoned lust for the feeling element … for the perception element … for the formation element … for the consciousness element — with the abandonment of lust, the basis is cut off, the support of consciousness does not exist. Without that support, consciousness does not expand, does not generate activity, and is liberated; being liberated, it is steady; being steady, it is content; being content, it is not agitated; being not agitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.54
